title: Chirp Pong
summary:
Tool: Chirp Pong 

 Another game experiment - I wanted to see if it was feasible to have a two player game on two separate phones running in static HTML where the networking code uses chirps sent via the microphone. It seems to work!

 Build a two player competitive pong like game where two players use their phones close to each other and the game state is sent via audio noises which the web microphone API can interpret - but add graphical and gameplay twists to make it a lot more fun and intertwine than pong

title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
summary:
At a glance 

 A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run.

 Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now.

 Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical.

 A new form of computing 

 Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust.

title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
summary:
Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO 

The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ".

 Key things I learned from the article:

 Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn"

 Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn

 Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn

 In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power"

 Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11%

 This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):

 The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.

 When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.

 Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

 Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter!

 Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to th

title: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents
summary: Multimodal agents commonly generate freeform reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from the reasoning candidates based on their…

title: Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
summary: Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry.
